title: RCD / breaker tripped
intro: Power out in part of the house? Find which circuit and which appliance tripped it, and reset.

steps.t: Go to the fuse box with a torch and find the switch that's down: the RCD (it has a T test button) or a breaker.
steps.w: Burning smell, smoke or a hot fuse box? Don't touch anything and call an electrician.

steps.t: Switch off all the individual circuit breakers next to the RCD.
Push the RCD back up firmly, all the way.
steps.fix: If it trips again with every circuit off, don't keep trying: leave it off and call an electrician.
steps.w: Never hold the switch up by force or tape it: it trips to protect you.

steps.t: Switch the circuits back on one at a time, a few seconds apart: the one that trips it is the faulty circuit.
Leave the faulty circuit off, reset the RCD and switch the rest back on: the rest of the house has power.
Unplug everything on the faulty circuit: the rooms that are still dark.
Now switch the faulty circuit back on, with everything still unplugged.
steps.q: Does the circuit stay on with nothing plugged in?
steps.fix: If it trips with nothing plugged in, the fault is in the wiring: leave it off and call an electrician.

steps.t: Plug the appliances back in one at a time: the one that trips it is the culprit.
Leave that appliance unplugged and get it repaired or replaced.

tips: Trips when it rains? Check outdoor sockets and garden lights: damp is a common cause.
Appliances with water and heating elements (washer, dishwasher, oven, water heater) are the usual culprits.
Press the RCD's T button about every six months: it should trip. If it doesn't, get it checked.

title: Replace a ceiling light
intro: Swap an old ceiling light for a new one on the same wiring, with the power off and tested.
gate: I'm replacing an existing light, not adding a new light point
I have a steady stepladder and someone to help hold the light

steps.t: At the fuse box or panel, switch off the lighting circuit for this room. The wall switch alone isn't enough.
steps.w: A wall switch may cut only one wire: always work with the circuit off at the panel.

steps.t: Open the stepladder fully under the light, on level floor, and don't stand on the top step.
steps.w: Don't stand on chairs or stools: with your arms up it's easy to lose your balance.

steps.t: Unscrew the canopy or shade of the old light and lower it, without touching the wires.
With the wall switch on, test every wire at the ceiling with the tester: no voltage.
steps.q: Does the tester show no voltage on every wire?
steps.fix: Don't touch anything: go back to the panel, switch off the main and test again.
steps.w: Check the tester on a working socket first. If it shows voltage, don't touch anything.

steps.t: Take a photo of the connections: which wire goes where, with colours and terminals.
Have someone hold the light, then disconnect the wires and remove the old light and its bracket.
steps.w: Never leave a light hanging by its wires: they pull out and it falls.

steps.t: Check the ceiling fixing: the hook or plugs must be solid and able to take the new light's weight.
steps.q: Is the fixing solid and right for the new light's weight?
steps.fix: If it moves or the light is heavy, redo the fixing with plugs suited to your ceiling before hanging it.

steps.t: Fix the new light's bracket or hook to the ceiling, following its instructions.
Connect the wires with the connectors as in the photo: earth (ground) to the light's earth terminal.
Tug each wire gently in the connectors and check there's no bare copper showing.
steps.q: Does every wire hold, with no bare copper showing?
steps.fix: Open the connector, strip the wire to the length marked on it (often [[10 mm]]) and close it again.

steps.t: Tuck the wires into the canopy without pinching them, hang the light, then fit the canopy and bulbs.
Switch the circuit back on at the panel and flick the wall switch: the light should come on and stay steady.

tips: Class II light (double-square symbol) with no earth terminal: cap the earth wire in its own connector.
Use lever connectors: they grip well, can be reopened and need no tape.
Heavy chandeliers or ceiling fans need special fixings or boxes: if unsure, ask an electrician.

title: Replace a wall socket (outlet)
intro: Cracked or loose socket? Swap it for an identical one, with the power off and tested.
gate: I'm replacing an identical socket, not adding a new one
I know which breaker feeds this socket
I have a voltage tester and know it works

mats.n: Socket (same type as the old one)

steps.t: At the fuse box or panel, switch off the breaker for this socket. Not sure which one? Switch off the main.
steps.w: Unplugging things isn't enough: the socket stays live until its breaker is off.

steps.t: Check the tester on a socket that works, then test every hole of this one: it must show no voltage.
steps.q: Does the tester show no voltage on every hole?
steps.fix: Don't touch anything: you switched off the wrong circuit. Go back, switch off the main and test again.
steps.w: If the tester shows voltage, or you're not sure it works, don't touch the socket.

steps.t: Undo the screws holding the socket or its cover and ease it out of the box without yanking the wires.
Test again right on the terminals, now exposed: still no voltage.
Take a close-up photo of the wiring: which wire, which colour, which terminal.
Loosen the terminals and free the wires one at a time. On push-in terminals, press the release tab.
Look at the wires and the box: clean copper, intact insulation, no scorch or melt marks.
steps.q: Are the wires and box intact, with no scorch marks?
steps.fix: Stop: leave the circuit off and call an electrician. Don't fit the new socket.

steps.t: Connect each wire to the matching terminal on the new socket, as in the photo, earth to earth, and tighten firmly.
Tug each wire gently: it must stay put, with no bare copper showing outside the terminal.
steps.q: Does every wire hold, with no bare copper showing?
steps.fix: Undo the terminal, strip or trim the wire to the length marked on the socket (often [[10 mm]]) and tighten again.

steps.t: Fold the wires neatly into the box, screw the socket in straight and refit the cover.
Switch the breaker back on at the panel.
Test the socket with a lamp. If the RCD trips or anything gets warm, switch off and call an electrician.

tips: Damaged wires, aluminium wiring (dull silver) or a blackened box: stop and call an electrician.
Take the old socket to the shop: the type, rating and fixing must match.
In older homes wire colours can't be trusted: copy the photo, not the colours.

title: New sockets, circuits or fuse box work
intro: Adding sockets, lights or circuits, or touching the fuse box: what to do before the pro comes.
why: New circuits and consumer unit work need correct cable sizes and protection, and by law a qualified electrician.

steps.t: Write down what you need: how many new sockets or lights, where, and for which appliances (oven, hob, A/C).
Photograph the fuse box as it is, without removing any covers: switches and labels. The electrician will need them.
If you smell burning or see black marks, switch off the main switch and touch nothing else.
steps.w: Don't open the fuse box: even with the main off, the incoming terminals stay live.

steps.t: Hire a registered electrician (Part P scheme in England, licensed in the US) and ask for the certificate at the end.
Keep the certificate with your house papers: you'll need it to sell, let or insure the home.

tips: Ask for a written quote listing the work: it makes comparing offers easy.
